explain.say: On the first of January 1970 the United States signed its National Environmental Policy Act, the first law to demand a study of a big project's effects on nature and people before it is approved. Now almost every country has one. Here is the path an environmental impact assessment, or EIA, follows.

explain.say: It starts with screening, lighting up now: does this project need a full EIA at all? Big motorways, dams and airports always do; a small shed does not. Then scoping picks the issues that really matter here, perhaps noise and a wetland, so the study does not drown in detail. Why not study every possible effect?

explain.say: Time and money are limited, so focus wins! Next comes the baseline study: measuring the site as it is now, its birds, air, noise, water and people. Only then can the team predict what the project will change, and by how much.

explain.say: How do they rank impacts? A simple way multiplies the size of the change, its magnitude, by how sensitive the thing affected is, each scored one to five. Noise of magnitude four near a school of sensitivity four scores sixteen. Losing a rare wetland scores the top, twenty five. Which impact needs the most attention?

The wetland! Mitigation follows a hierarchy: first avoid the harm, perhaps by moving the road, then reduce it, then restore, and only last offset it elsewhere. Then people are consulted, a decision is made, and monitoring checks the promises are kept. Superb! Challenge: what would you do first for the wetland?

faq.q: What is an environmental impact assessment?
faq.a: A formal study of a proposed project's likely effects on the environment and people, carried out before a decision is made, with public consultation and measures to reduce harm.
Screening decides whether a project needs a full EIA, using lists and thresholds of size and location. Large dams, motorways and airports usually need one automatically.
asks: Does my project need an EIA?

faq.a: Scoping identifies the important issues and the study area so the assessment focuses on the impacts that are likely to be significant.

faq.q: How is the significance of an impact judged?
faq.a: Often by combining the magnitude of the change with the sensitivity of the receptor, for example scoring each from 1 to 5 and multiplying. A score of 16 or more might be called major.
An order of action against harm: avoid first, then minimise, then restore, and offset only what remains.

facts: The US National Environmental Policy Act was signed on 1 January 1970.
The European Union adopted its first EIA Directive in 1985.
India's EIA Notification of 2006 sorts projects into categories A and B.
